name: Fatal Infantile Cytochrome C Oxidase Deficiency
aliases: Fatal Infantile Mitochondrial Complex IV Deficiency

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Mitochondrial Disease Diagnostic Criteria (MDC) adapted for COX deficiency

criteria.description: Progressive encephalopathy with hypotonia and developmental regression in infancy
Deficient cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV) activity in muscle or fibroblasts
Pathogenic variants in nuclear or mitochondrial genes encoding cytochrome c oxidase subunits or assembly factors
Brain MRI showing cerebral atrophy and basal ganglia abnormalities
Elevated lactate levels in blood and/or cerebrospinal fluid

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of progressive infantile encephalopathy with biochemical evidence of cytochrome c oxidase deficiency and genetic confirmation or muscle biopsy findings
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis requires integration of clinical, biochemical, and genetic data due to phenotypic variability.

pathognomonic.notes: Rapid neurodegeneration leading to severe developmental delay
Profound muscle weakness apparent in early infancy
Metabolic acidosis due to mitochondrial dysfunction

common.notes: Poor weight gain and growth retardation
Progressive respiratory failure due to muscle weakness
Generalized or focal seizures in infancy
Impaired eye movement due to extraocular muscle involvement

occasional.notes: Hypertrophic or dilated cardiomyopathy reported in some cases
Enlarged liver due to metabolic stress
Hearing impairment secondary to mitochondrial dysfunction

rare.notes: Rare skin changes such as livedo reticularis
Irritability and abnormal behavior in late stages

laboratory: Elevated blood and CSF lactate and pyruvate levels
Reduced cytochrome c oxidase enzyme activity in muscle biopsy
Metabolic acidosis with elevated anion gap
imaging: Brain MRI showing cerebral atrophy, basal ganglia signal abnormalities, and delayed myelination
Cardiac echocardiogram revealing cardiomyopathy in some cases
genetic: Pathogenic mutations in mitochondrial DNA-encoded COX subunits (e.g., MT-CO1, MT-CO2, MT-CO3)
other: Muscle biopsy showing ragged red fibers and COX-negative fibers

distinguishingFeatures: Subacute necrotizing encephalomyelopathy with characteristic MRI lesions in basal ganglia and brainstem
Broader genetic heterogeneity including complex I and II deficiencies
Predominantly muscle involvement with exercise intolerance
Less severe infantile encephalopathy and variable COX activity

redFlags: Rapidly progressive neurodegeneration in early infancy
Severe lactic acidosis refractory to treatment
Early onset respiratory failure requiring ventilatory support
references: DiMauro S, Schon EA. Mitochondrial respiratory-chain diseases. N Engl J Med. 2003 Jun 19;348(26):2656-68.
Tiranti V, et al. SURF1 mutations in Leigh syndrome associated with cytochrome c oxidase deficiency. Am J Hum Genet. 1998 Jul;63(1):160-6.
Rahman S, et al. Leigh syndrome: clinical features and biochemical and DNA abnormalities. Ann Neurol. 1996 Sep;40(3):339-47.
